A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same semantic alphabet-size and entropy estimators. All 18 pages of v1 and 22 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable; equations, tables, figures and relocated content support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original entropy-estimation, incorrectness-detection and human-annotated semantic-clustering results, including Tables 1–3 and Figures 2–7.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds results for Gemma-3-12B, clustering comparators, sampling diagnostics and semantic probability-distribution comparisons.

M1.justification: The proposed hybrid alphabet-size and coverage-adjusted entropy estimators remain unchanged in Equations 9–10. Both versions use NLI-NQ bidirectional entailment clustering for the main experiments. Newly evaluated embedding-based clustering methods are comparators.

E1.justification: Both versions use HotpotQA, SQuAD 2.0, BioASQ and POTATO for the same QA uncertainty and semantic-clustering tasks. The additional model, larger HotpotQA sample and new diagnostics remain within this existing data and task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds white-box SE to the incorrectness comparison and sample-size plots; v1 used it as the entropy reference but omitted it from these comparator sets. Table 2 also expands beyond LLM and NLI-NQ clustering to include embedding-based HDBSCAN and DBSCAN at four radii. These substantially broaden two comparison sets.

E3.justification: v2 adds Gemma-3-12B. The reported HotpotQA setting changes from 1,852 examples to all 7,405 for incorrectness detection, while entropy-estimation experiments use the first 25%. Table 2 replaces the combined |S| >= 1 evaluation with a separate |S| = 1 stratum. New diagnostics introduce ten-sample batches, KL/TVD/MAE comparisons and an SE* < 0.005 exclusion sensitivity check.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing sample-size and regularization analyses, v2 adds information-gain evidence for the 100-sample reference (Appendix C), diagnosis and filtering of extreme entropy-ratio cases (D), empirical-frequency versus RBMCI distribution comparisons (E), and direct alphabet-size underestimation analysis (G). Appendix A.3 also expands clustering diagnostics against human annotations.

E5.justification: Both versions report MSE confidence intervals using standard errors, DeLong AUROC intervals, 100 simulated matches per method pair and model-dataset setting, and Bradley–Terry strength/rank intervals. v2 retains these procedures; changed interval values and additional result entries do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds Gemma-3-12B and revises existing values, such as Llama-3.1/SQuAD plugin MSE from 0.84 to 0.78. Under the revised comparison suite, the hybrid alphabet estimator's rank interval changes from [1, 2] to [1, 4], while U_EigV changes from [3, 4] to [1, 3] and has the highest strength estimate. These are revised results, not established same-setting gains. New diagnostics also report overshooting cases and close SE/DSE probability distributions.

T1.justification: The mathematical substance of Equations 1–14, the Zipfian argument in Appendix B and the rank-interval construction in Appendix A.6 is retained. The added empirical-frequency expression after Equation 8 spells out an existing quantity. The new empirical diagnostics introduce no substantive theorem, proof or derivation.

C1.justification: v1 claims that its proposed alphabet estimator matches or exceeds all nine comparators. v2 reframes this central contribution around two alphabet estimators, including the existing U_EigV, performing competitively with most alternatives, and acknowledges U_EigV's leading strength estimate. It also extends the hybrid entropy estimator's incorrectness-detection claim to comparison with white-box SE.

C2.justification: v2 explains how early sampling of rare categories can exaggerate tail mass and cause hybrid entropy overshooting, qualifying v1's predominantly downward-bias interpretation. It argues that sequence probabilities help white-box SE down-weight these events and interprets the otherwise similar SE/DSE distributions (Appendices D–E). Appendix C supplies an empirical rationale for the retained reference assumption.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds the embedding model identifier and access link, cosine-distance specification, and DBSCAN radii 0.05, 0.075, 0.1 and 0.15. Section 6.3 adds reproducibility pointers. Existing generation limits, prompts, temperatures, NLI model and core estimator settings are largely retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Gemma 3, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, KL divergence and total variation distance. Appendix A.5 clarifies why the evaluated SNNE and KLE configurations are not classified as explicit SE estimators. The broader related-work framework in Section 5 remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and method exposition are retained. v2 refines SE/DSE terminology, locally rewrites the results and conclusion, moves the n=10 explanation from Appendix A.1 to Section 4.1, adds a reproducibility subsection, relabels the LLM-use disclosure and reorganizes the expanded appendices.

P2.justification: v2 adds diagnostic Figures 6, 8, 9 and 11 and Table 4. Existing displays expand to accommodate five models and eleven uncertainty methods, while Table 2 gains grouped embedding-comparator rows and revised evaluation columns. The ranking plot and heatmap exchange figure numbers and the heatmap moves to the following page. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification through reference-sample diagnostics, white-box and clustering comparisons, and explicit analysis of an estimator failure case. It also recalibrates v1's superiority claim to acknowledge U_EigV's stronger showing. The 100-sample reference remains a proxy, and minor presentation errors persist, including Figure 3's ten-method caption despite eleven plotted methods. Nevertheless, the added diagnostics and better-qualified conclusions substantially improve the paper's evidential support.
